docs.title: SatellaStory
docs.text: Welcome to SatellaStory -- a comprehensive historical documentation project dedicated to preserving the history, lore, and community of the Nintendo Satellaview satellite modem system for the Super Famicom, with special emphasis on BS-X: Sore wa Namae o Nusumareta Machi no Monogatari (BS-X: The Story of the Town Whose Name Was Stolen).

docs.title: About This Project
docs.text: This archive is the result of systematic historical research into the Satellaview ecosystem -- its technology, its games, its people, and its community. Every piece of information presented here is sourced from verifiable references including archived web pages, blog posts, forum discussions, official documents, and primary source accounts.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
• Satellaview System -- The satellite modem accessory for the Super Famicom (1995-2000)
  • St.GIGA -- The radio broadcaster that partnered with Nintendo
  • BS-X Cartridge -- The operating system/browser cartridge that served as the gateway to all Satellaview content
  • Broadcast Games -- SoundLink and downloadable games
  • Community -- The fan communities that formed during and after the service
  • Preservation -- Restoration projects, ROM dumping, and emulation efforts

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
All information in this archive is sourced from:

  1. Primary sources (archived web pages, forum posts, blog entries, official documentation)
  2. Secondary sources (wiki articles, retrospective analyses)
  3. Direct community records (IRC logs, email archives, preserved websites)

Each claim is annotated with a reference number linking to the References page, which provides the full citation and where applicable, the Wayback Machine archival link.

docs.title: Fan Projects Overview
docs.text: Since the time of the last Satellaview broadcast, numerous fan sites and projects have emerged to memorialize the system and preserve its content. Due to the Satellaview's Japan-only release, the overwhelming majority of early fan sites were Japanese-language.1

docs.title: The Preservation Challenge
docs.text: The dissolution of St.GIGA and Nintendo's attempts to distance itself from what has been considered a failed system, combined with the inevitable progress of subsequent technologies, has resulted in much of the information that once existed on the system being lost to time. Modern sites serve quasi-archeological purposes and engage in historical research.2

docs.title: Community Structure
docs.text:
The Satellaview community can be divided into several overlapping groups:

Community Type Description Historical Japanese Sites from the active broadcast era (1995-2000) and immediate post-service period Modern Japanese Blogs and wikis maintained by Japanese enthusiasts documenting the system English-Language Primarily the Satellablog, BS Zelda Shrine, and English Satellaview Wiki Technical/Preservation ROM dumping, emulation, signal simulation, and restoration projects

docs.title: Key Principles
docs.text: The community generally operates under shared values: - Restoration should aim for accuracy to original materials (though disagreements exist) - Content should be shared freely, not sold for profit - Profiteering (e.g., eBay sales of restored material) is widely condemned3 - Communication between language groups is encouraged but often challenging4

docs.title: Restoration Approaches
docs.text: Restoration groups can be divided into: 1. Purists -- seek to restore original material in as accurate-to-the-original a manner as possible 2. Innovators -- seek to restore a semblance of the original game, sometimes incorporating modern innovations 3. Expansionists -- introduce Satellaview elements to non-Satellaview games (e.g., inserting the BS-X avatar into A Link to the Past)5

docs.title: The SatellaOFF Events (1999)
docs.text: The SatellaOFF events were the first known real-life meetups of Satellaview enthusiasts, occurring at the very end of the Satellaview's active lifetime and continuing for a brief period after broadcasts ceased. The name is a pun: "Satella" (Satellaview) + "OFF" (offline meeting, as opposed to online).1

docs.title: Historical Significance
docs.text:
The SatellaOFF pages contain a St.GIGA Data Broadcast Timeline (1995-1999) tracking the shift from normal data broadcasts to Sound Link games to the Satellaview Guide, ending with broadcast cessation around June 1999. This makes them a primary source for the service's chronology.5

HIRO maintained exhaustive diaries with ~25+ photos per event. The pages also feature character illustrations of all attendees drawn by Blackeye, creator of the BS-X no Hanashi site.6

Additional participant reports were created by other attendees: - Mizota: "Mizota's Secret Diary March 28-29" on his site KIMATTA!13 - Halki Hiro: "BS SatellaOFF War Report" on Rakuho-so, with detailed per-item commentary14 - Pane-pon-master: "Finally! Satellaview OFF!!" with a humorous post-event writeup15 - Yulil: "Sound Novel - SatellaOFF" featuring extensive Sound Novel-style narrative of the event16

The SatellaOFF event was first announced via the "BS-X no Hanashi" site's bulletin board, posted by St.GIGA themselves. The six webmasters who attended represented the entire active Satellaview fan community at the time.6

docs.title: BS-X Cult (Late 1990s -- Early 2000s)
docs.text: BS-X Cult was a Satellaview ROM site from the late 1990s maintained by Pachuka (also known as RealaNightmaren). It was an offshoot of Pachuka's earlier EmuCult website, a general emulation site founded around 1999.7

docs.title: The ROMar Connection
docs.text:
Pachuka claimed to have stolen the ROMs hosted on BS-X Cult from a person known as ROMar. ROMar is believed to have been the source of:8

  • The BS Dragon Quest prototype (a unique build with all 4 weeks combined in a single ROM with a debug episode-select menu and valid BS-X checksum)
  • The BS Zelda no Densetsu ROMs (Map 1 and Map 2)
  • Potentially the BS Zelda no Densetsu: Inishie no Sekiban ROMs

ROMar's true identity has never been discovered. Satellablog author KiddoCabbusses attempted to track ROMar down through Pachuka but was unsuccessful. When asked for details, Pachuka was unresponsive and demonstrated poor knowledge of the games he had leaked.9

docs.title: Pachuka's Legacy
docs.text:
Pachuka's larger site X-Cult (x-cult.org) expanded to cover game prototypes across multiple platforms. The site went through several iterations including Sonic CulT (1999), which became the largest Sonic prototype research site of its era. Pachuka was reportedly arrested in the early 2000s for sexual assault of minors, and site ownership transferred to Sazpaimon.10

As of 2026, x-cult.org displays only "IT'S OVER" and appears permanently defunct.11

docs.title: The Original Satellablog (2008-2009)
docs.text:
The Satellablog was founded in April 2008 at satellablog.blogspot.com by the user known as KiddoCabbusses ("Kiddo"). Its stated objectives were:12

  1. Spread information about the Satellaview
  2. Correct misinformation already present on the web
  3. Host videos of unreleased games and archived radio programs

The blog maintainer made significant efforts toward international communication by: - Linking to auto-translation tools - Writing posts partially in Japanese - Welcoming comments in any language - Maintaining an IRC channel (#serioushax on Caffienet)17

In April 2009, the blog relocated to superfamicom.org/blog due to technical difficulties and accuracy concerns.18 The last update by KiddoCabbusses was August 26, 2009.

docs.title: Key Achievements
docs.text:
• Documented the history of Satellaview emulation and ROM dumping19
  • Exposed eBay profiteering from restored Satellaview content20
  • Connected the international Satellaview community
  • Launched The English Satellaview Wiki (September 2009)21
  • Coordinated with LuigiBlood, Matthew Callis, and d4s22

The blog was revived in 2024-2026 by a new maintainer, danyl, who now posts regular Satellaview ROM dumps and memory pack content.23

docs.title: BS-X Project (LuigiBlood)
docs.text:
Started in September 2010 by LuigiBlood (then known as Seru-kun), the BS-X Project (originally "Broadcast Satellaview") aims to restore complete functionality to the BS-X interface cartridge by simulating a satellite broadcast signal.1

Key achievements:

Achievement Year Details "Hello Satellaview!" homebrew 2010 First Satellaview homebrew application; reverse-engineered the BS-X header format2 English Translation Patch v1.3 2016 Full English translation of the BS-X town interface; "No DRM" variant available3 SatellaWave v0.5.1 2019 Satellaview Server Manager (C#, MIT) for creating broadcast data binary files4 bsnes-plus integration 2016 Proper BS-X mapper emulation, Memory Pack support (Type 1 Flash commands)5 SNES9X support 2017 Upstreamed Satellaview emulation into official SNES9X (v1.55+)6 sd2snes/FX Pak Pro 2014+ Real-hardware Satellaview emulation via flashcarts7

The project also contributed to: - Memory Pack patches for RPG Tsukuru 2 and Sound Novel Tsukuru (fixing Data Pack loading)8 - Satellaview technical documentation on the Super Famicom development wiki9 - IRC collaboration logs archived on the dev wiki10

docs.title: d4s Signal Simulation
docs.text: German programmer Matthias Nagler (d4s) was the first to attempt BS-X signal simulation, documenting the Satellaview's base modem register map and how the satellite stream protocol worked. His BS Excitebike patch (2006) was the first to modify a Satellaview SoundLink ROM to function without satellite input.11

docs.title: BS Zelda no Densetsu (Map 1 and Map 2)
docs.text:
The BS Zelda Shrine (founded November 2, 1999 by Con) has been the central hub for BS Zelda restoration. Dumped ROM material from both Map 1 and Map 2 has been recovered and released as real-hardware-compatible ROMs.12

Notable restoration achievements: - Full restoration of all 4 weeks for both Map 1 ("Third Quest") and Map 2 ("Fourth Quest") - MSU-1 audio enhancement patches - Subtitles for original voice-over material - English translation of voice-over text13

Con (contact: con.s@gmx.de) declared the site's mission complete in 2016: "The mission this site began in 1999 is with this release accomplished!" -- but returned for smaller updates through 2020, including new bosses (Lanmola, Gleeok), Darkshade's intro screen polish, and Link version improvements.14

docs.title: BS Zelda no Densetsu: Inishie no Sekiban (Ancient Stone Tablets)
docs.text:
The Ancient Stone Tablets (AST) was a SoundLink game broadcast in 1997-1998, functioning as a sequel to A Link to the Past. The game was restored by: - Duke Serkol (FAQ author, storyline documentation, AST indoor area recreation using Euclid's editor) - Con (AST Master Quest creation, MSU-1 patches) - Hackers from the BS Zelda Shrine community

The game was reconstructed from VHS-recorded broadcasts and the only known week 3 ROM dump.15

docs.title: Master Quest Event (2009)
docs.text: On April 11, 2009, the BS Zelda Shrine held a timed competition through a modified hard version of AST called the "Master Quest." Scoring followed the original April 1997 broadcast rules. Winner: Phoenix (phoenix20xx@gmail.com), who received an entry in the Hall of Fame.16

docs.title: BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki
docs.text:
The 4-episode SoundLink series (broadcast September 28-October 19, 1997) has seen several restoration attempts:

  • 2009: A mod/mock-up using SRPG Maker 9517
  • 2009: Fan-driven pressure on Intelligent Systems led to official comment from the original developer18
  • Subsequent: The game was eventually re-released for the Nintendo DS
  • Fan music restoration from VHS recordings (via Nico Nico Douga)19

The BS Fire Emblem page by imoko documented a fan-compiled voice actor cast list with listener collaboration.20

docs.title: BS Tantei Club: Yuki ni Kieru Kako
docs.text: A fan project called "Project Gam" was formed to restore this game. Several attempts to restore the original Satellaview music were also made from period VHS recordings.21

docs.title: Music and Audio Restoration
docs.text:
Music restoration has been a recurring theme across multiple games. The approach typically involves: 1. Recording broadcasts to VHS tape in real time 2. Extracting audio portions 3. Splitting "clean" segments into contiguous wholes 4. Matching restored audio to game events22

Games with significant music restoration efforts: - BS Zelda series (album-sourced music also available)23 - BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki - BS Tantei Club: Yuki ni Kieru Kako - BS Shin Onigashima24

docs.title: Satellaview+ Revival Project
docs.text:
The Satellaview+ project (at satellaviewplus.github.io) is a more recent effort that spins up from the BS-X Project's infrastructure. It aims to reconnect users to a simulated St.GIGA broadcast server, allowing original Satellaview hardware or emulators to "receive" broadcasts as they would have in 1995-2000. The project leverages SatellaWave export format and bsnes-plus emulation.25

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Satellaview hosted a diverse library of games and content across multiple formats. This section catalogs known broadcast games with available information.

docs.title: SoundLink Games
docs.text:
Real-time interactive games synchronized with live radio broadcasts. These featured voice acting, narration, music, and live commentary. SoundLink games were inherently ephemeral -- they played during specific broadcast windows and could not be saved.1

Examples: BS Zelda: Inishie no Sekiban, BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki, BS Tantei Club, BS F-Zero Grand Prix

docs.title: Downloadable Games
docs.text: Full games that could be downloaded to the Memory Pack and played at any time after broadcast. Some were Satellaview-exclusive; others were modified versions of existing Super Famicom titles.2

docs.title: Add-On Data
docs.text: Additional content or levels for existing Super Famicom games, distributed via satellite.

docs.title: Magazines and "Kabe Shinbun"
docs.text: Downloadable magazines and "wall newspaper" content that provided news, tips, game journalism, and broadcast schedules.3

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: BS Dragon Quest was a Satellaview broadcast of Dragon Quest-themed content. It is notable primarily for the existence of a unique debug ROM that contains all 4 broadcast weeks combined into a single file with an episode-select menu and a valid BS-X checksum.1

docs.title: The Debug ROM
docs.text:
The BS Dragon Quest ROM was part of the stash leaked by Pachuka from ROMar and hosted on BS-X Cult. It is unusual because:

  • It contains all 4 weeks in one file with a debug menu
  • It has a valid BS-X checksum (highly unusual for hacks or modified ROMs)
  • It was NOT modified for emulator compatibility (unlike most early Satellaview ROM hacks)2

This suggests the ROM may have been an internal development or QA build rather than a consumer release.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text: The origin of the BS Dragon Quest ROM is one of the Satellaview's enduring mysteries. The debug features suggest it came from a development environment, but how ROMar obtained it and who created it is unknown. Satellablog author KiddoCabbusses investigated the ROM's origins extensively but was unable to determine more than what Pachuka shared -- and Pachuka was deliberately vague.3

docs.title: Current Status
docs.text:
The BS Dragon Quest ROM has been dumped and is preserved. It remains one of the most unusual Satellaview artifacts due to its combined-week format and debug features.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki (BSファイアーエムブレム アカネイア戦記) was a SoundLink game broadcast in 1997. It consisted of 4 episodes combining radio drama segments with tactical RPG gameplay, set in the world of the original Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light.1

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Each episode was structured as: 1. Drama segment -- Radio drama advancing the story 2. Game system explanation -- Tutorial narrated by personalities 3. Map battle -- Tactical RPG gameplay synchronized with broadcast 4. Drama segment -- Conclusion and setup for next episode2

As a SoundLink game, BS Fire Emblem could not be saved to the Memory Pack. It existed only during the broadcast window.3

docs.title: Connections to Main Series
docs.text: The game's ending teased Thracia 776, which would later be released as a full Super Famicom game. Intelligent Systems (Intsys) acknowledged fan interest in the game in 2009 after community-driven pressure. The game was eventually re-released for the Nintendo DS with updated presentation.4

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BS Zelda series consists of three distinct Satellaview games based on The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past. These games were among the most popular Satellaview titles and have received significant fan restoration efforts.1

docs.title: BS Zelda no Densetsu (Map 1: "Third Quest")
docs.text:
The first BS Zelda game featured a modified version of A Link to the Past's overworld with new dungeon layouts. The dungeon names spell "St.GIGA":2

Week Dungeon Theme Week 1 S Week 2 t Week 3 . Week 4 GIGA

Each week was broadcast separately and required the player to complete the dungeon within the broadcast period. The game was downloadable and could be played between broadcasts.3

docs.title: BS Zelda no Densetsu (Map 2: "Fourth Quest")

The sequel map featured even harder dungeons. The dungeon names spell "NiNtENDO":4

docs.title: BS Zelda no Densetsu: Inishie no Sekiban (Ancient Stone Tablets)
docs.text: The most complex of the BS Zelda titles, Ancient Stone Tablets (AST) was a SoundLink game -- the first Zelda game with full voice acting and a live radio drama component. The game was broadcast in 1997-1998 as the centerpiece of St.GIGA's Satellaview programming.5

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
• SoundLink format -- required live radio broadcast; could not be saved to Memory Pack
  • Featured voice actors performing character dialogue in real time
  • Music and sound effects synchronized with radio broadcast
  • Functioned as a direct sequel to A Link to the Past6

docs.title: Story
docs.text: The game takes place six years after A Link to the Past. A new villain named Grah appears and Link must once again save Hyrule. The game introduced new items, puzzles, and a scoring system that ranked players based on performance.7

docs.title: Scoring System
docs.text:
• Deaths: -10,000 points each
  • Rupees: +10 points each
  • Heart Containers and tablets auto-calculated
  • Result screens at end of each week calculated scores automatically8

docs.title: ROM Dumping
docs.text: The BS Zelda ROMs have a complex dumping history. The first known dumps came from BS-X Cult (via Pachuka/ROMar) and were among the first Satellaview ROMs to hit the internet. Multiple revisions and versions have been identified; some versions have undumped corruption (e.g., week 3 of Map 1 had 0x28CC7: 0x02 instead of 0x00 per LuigiBlood's analysis).9

docs.title: BS Zelda Shrine (1999-2020)
docs.text:
The BS Zelda Shrine, founded November 2, 1999 by Con, has been the primary hub for BS Zelda restoration. Key milestones:

  • Full restoration of Map 1 and Map 2 as real-hardware-compatible ROMs10
  • English translation of in-game text
  • Voice-over subtitle patches
  • MSU-1 audio enhancement patches
  • Master Quest hard mode (2009)
  • AST Master Quest competition (April 2009)11

docs.title: Translation Efforts
docs.text: The BS Zelda games featured voice-over dialogue that was never subtitled. Fan translation projects have worked to: - Transcribe all voice-over material - Create English subtitle patches - Translate Japanese text in menus and item descriptions12

docs.title: Music Restoration
docs.text: The BS Zelda music has been restored from multiple sources: - VHS recordings of original broadcasts (audio extraction and splicing)13 - Album sources -- official soundtrack releases that contained BS Zelda music14 - MSU-1 patches -- replacing restoration-enhanced music in the ROMs15

docs.text:

  • BS Zelda Map 1 — annotated complete run (YouTube, 4 parts): subtitled gameplay with original Japanese voice acting18
  • BS Zelda Map 1 — makuchan's video (YouTube): shows how a SoundLink game was downloaded and played during the original broadcast19
  • BS Zelda: Ancient Stone Tablets — week 4 voice acting translation (BS Zelda Shrine): full transcript synced to original broadcast video20
  • BS Zelda: Ancient Stone Tablets — all weeks (NicoVideo): discovered 2007, contains complete voice acting and music21
  • English dub project (Nintendo Life, 2016): fan-produced English voice acting replacement for Map 1 and Ancient Stone Tablets22

docs.title: Tamori no Picross
docs.text:
Developed by Jupiter Corporation and published by Nintendo. A Picross (nonogram) puzzle game hosted by the famous Japanese television personality Tamori (Kazuyoshi Morita). Broadcast from April to September 1995.6

Date controversy: Jupiter's official page states the broadcast was August 6 - September 2, 1995. However, SFC Mania (randnetdd) investigated this using original VHS recordings and proved this was incorrect:7

  • VHS evidence shows broadcasts on April 23, 1995 (Satellaview launch day) and June 8, 1995, predating Jupiter's claimed dates
  • SFC Mania identified 4 different title screens for the game, suggesting multiple broadcast periods or versions
  • The April 23 broadcast lacked the "Obake" and "Yasashii" Picross modes that appeared in later versions
  • The earliest known VHS recording from April 23, 1995 features only 45 puzzles and different BGM
  • Later recordings show 60 puzzles, new BGMs, and different screen layouts
  • SFC Mania's conclusion: "Jupiter's data absolutely has mistakes" -- the actual broadcast period was longer and started earlier than officially documented

The game featured: - Normal Picross, Obake (Ghost) Picross (time-limited), and Yasashii (Easy) Picross modes - Tamori's character provided voice commentary during gameplay - Comic strip illustrations by artist "Yoshida Senpai" were submitted by viewers and featured in the game - A "Tamori's Happy Set" pen was given as a prize to winners of the picross competitions

SFC Mania also noted the game's BGM was very similar to standard Mario BGM but with slight differences in pitch and arrangement, and that the game lacked the extra hidden content found in the retail Mario no Picross.

docs.title: BS-X: The Story of the Town Whose Name Was Stolen
Overview
docs.text:
BS-X: Sore wa Namae o Nusumareta Machi no Monogatari (BS-X: それは名前を盗まれた街の物語, "BS-X: The Story of the Town Whose Name Was Stolen") was the operating system and user interface cartridge for the Satellaview system. Rather than a conventional menu, it presented itself as a fully realized game world -- a small town that the player could explore, populated by quirky characters, and filled with interactive elements.1

The game was developed by Nintendo in collaboration with St.GIGA and was released on April 23, 1995 as a launch title for the Satellaview system.2

docs.title: Premise
docs.text:
The player character arrives at a town whose name has been stolen by a mysterious entity. The townspeople cannot remember what the town was called. The player's task is to explore the town, interact with its residents, and participate in events to gradually restore the town's identity -- all while using the town as a hub to access Satellaview's broadcast features.3

The game's central location is Ransei Bridge (らんせい橋), where the player begins their journey. From there, they can access all areas of the town.4

docs.title: Gameplay
docs.text: Unlike a traditional game, BS-X functioned as a graphical operating system:

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
The player moved their avatar through a 2D top-down town using the D-pad. The town was divided into several districts, each offering different services:5

  • Event Plaza - Time-limited downloadable events and content
  • Download Center - Browse and download broadcasted games and data
  • Memory Pack Manager - Manage saved content on the Memory Pack
  • Magazine Stand - Access downloadable game magazines and news
  • Save/Configuration - Player name, gender, and system settings

docs.title: Player Avatar
docs.text:
Players configured their name and gender at the start. This determined the appearance of their in-game avatar:6

  • Male - Character wearing a backward baseball cap and a blue outfit
  • Female - Character with a pink ponytail and a pink/white outfit

This avatar would carry into many Satellaview broadcast games where supported, including the BS Zelda series and BS Fire Emblem.7

docs.title: Real-Time Features
docs.text:
BS-X was designed around the Satellaview's broadcast schedule. The town changed based on:

  • Time of day - Different characters appeared at different hours
  • Day of week - Certain events were only available on specific days
  • Broadcast schedule - Downloadable content appeared during and after broadcasts
  • Seasonal events - Holiday-themed content was broadcast periodically8

docs.title: The Satellaview Guide
docs.text: In later years (1997-1999), St.GIGA shifted to broadcasting primarily Satellaview Guide content -- a service that provided news, game tips, and magazine-style articles rather than full game downloads. This was reflected in the BS-X interface through updated town content.9

docs.title: The Name and Identity Theme
docs.text: The central metaphor of BS-X -- a town whose name has been stolen -- reflects the ephemeral nature of the Satellaview service itself. The town exists in a state of lost identity, much like the system's content would later become "lost" after broadcasts ceased. This theme has resonated strongly with preservationists working to recover and document the system's history.10

docs.title: BS-X in Emulation
docs.text:
The BS-X cartridge was initially difficult to emulate due to its custom mapper and the need for satellite signal simulation. The first BS-X BIOS emulation became available on September 24, 2004 via custom emulator builds.11

LuigiBlood's BS-X Project (started 2010) was the first comprehensive attempt to fake a satellite signal, allowing the BS-X cartridge to function in emulators as if receiving live broadcasts. The project produced:12

  • An English translation patch (final version v1.3, 2016)
  • The SatellaWave server manager for creating broadcast data
  • Emulation support in bsnes-plus and SNES9X
  • sd2snes/FX Pak Pro real-hardware support

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
BS-X remains one of the most distinctive operating systems in video game history -- a full game world that also functioned as a console's dashboard. Its approach of embedding system functionality within a narrative setting was unique for its time and remains rare to this day. The complete source code for the BS-X town interface has never been released, and the game survives today only through ROM dumps of retail cartridges and fan preservation efforts.13

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The town of BS-X is populated by a cast of distinctive characters who provide services, information, and personality to the interface. The following information has been compiled from archived fan sites, the BS Zelda Shrine, the Satellaview History Museum's map, and the Japanese Satellaview Wiki.1

Incomplete Data

Due to the loss of original source materials, some character names and details may be incomplete or reconstructed from multiple sources.

docs.title: The Player Avatar
docs.text:
The player character is the unnamed protagonist who arrives in the town. Their appearance is determined by the gender selected at configuration:2

  • Male Avatar -- Wears a backward red baseball cap, blue shirt, and blue pants
  • Female Avatar -- Wears a pink dress/outfit with a pink ponytail

The avatar renders in a small chibi-style sprite that can walk through the town, interact with NPCs, and access services. The same avatar model appears in broadcast games including BS Zelda and BS Fire Emblem when launched from the BS-X cartridge.3

docs.title: The Postman (Mail Delivery NPC)
docs.text: Located near the town entrance. Delivers broadcast notifications and system messages. Described by the Satellaview History Museum as the first NPC the player encounters.4

docs.title: The Old Man at the Download Center
docs.text: Manages the game and data download functionality. Players speak to him to browse available broadcasts and initiate downloads.5

docs.title: The Fortune Teller
docs.text: Provides broadcast schedule information and sometimes cryptic hints about upcoming content. Located in a dedicated stall in the town square.6

docs.title: The Bulletin Board Keeper
docs.text: Maintains the "kabe shinbun" (wall newspaper) -- a broadcast newspaper with news, tips, and game information that updated regularly via satellite.7

docs.title: Shopkeepers and Vendors
docs.text: Various unnamed vendors around the town sell or provide access to different services: - Memory Pack management services - Event Plaza access - Magazine downloads8

docs.title: Seasonal and Time-Limited Characters
docs.text: BS-X featured characters that only appeared during specific times or events: - Holiday characters -- Appeared during seasonal broadcasts (Christmas, New Year, etc.) - Event-specific NPCs -- Temporary characters that appeared during special promotions - The SatellaQuiz host -- Appeared during quiz broadcast events9

docs.title: The "Oshougatsu-san" NPC
docs.text: The NPC named "oshougatsu-san" appeared during the SatellaQuiz segments of the SatellaOFF events, functioning as a quiz opponent with a score of 232/500 in the recorded session. This NPC's name translates approximately to "New Year's person," suggesting it may have been a seasonal character.10

docs.title: Character Art
docs.text:
The only known original fan illustrations of the Satellaview community characters were drawn by Blackeye (webmaster of "BS-X no Hanashi") for the SatellaOFF event pages. These include portraits of the event attendees in a chibi style, which likely drew inspiration from the BS-X avatar design language.11 No official BS-X character art has been released by Nintendo.

docs.title: Memory Pack System
docs.text:
The Memory Pack (1 megabit / 128KB flash RAM) was the physical storage medium for all Satellaview content. It plugged into the BS-X cartridge and stored:1

  • Downloaded games
  • Save data
  • System configuration
  • Broadcast schedules

The Memory Pack used a combination of flash memory (for game storage) and battery-backed SRAM (for save data). This dual approach was necessary because flash memory was still relatively new and expensive for consumer devices in 1995.2

docs.title: Download Mechanics
docs.text:
Games and content were broadcast during specific time windows. The player navigated the BS-X town to the Download Center where they could:3

  • Browse available broadcasts (current and upcoming)
  • Initiate downloads during broadcast windows
  • View download progress and completion status
  • Launch downloaded games

Downloads were transmitted as part of the St.GIGA satellite signal. The BS-X cartridge contained the necessary decryption and decoding logic to convert the satellite data into usable game content.4

docs.title: The Avatar System
docs.text:
The player avatar chosen in BS-X served as a persistent character that carried into many broadcast games. This was a unique feature for its time:5

  • The avatar's appearance (male or female) was determined by gender selection
  • The avatar's name was set during initial configuration
  • Supported games would read the avatar data from the Memory Pack
  • Not all broadcast games supported this feature

docs.title: BS-X Items
docs.text:
The BS-X town featured various interactive items that could be found and sometimes purchased. Below are items documented by Satellaview Heaven:

These items were likely used in the town for transportation or decoration purposes, though the exact mechanics of many items remain undocumented.

docs.title: Broadcast Schedules
docs.text:
The BS-X town displayed current and upcoming broadcast schedules through various means:6

  • Fortune Teller NPC -- Provided broadcast schedule information
  • Bulletin Boards -- Displayed current and upcoming broadcasts
  • Kabe Shinbun -- Wall newspaper with news and game information
  • In-town NPCs -- Some characters provided scheduling hints

docs.title: Memory / Save Management
docs.text:
The Memory Pack had limited capacity (128KB). Players needed to manage their storage by:7

  • Deleting old games to make room for new downloads
  • Deciding which save data to retain
  • Removing magazines and other non-game content

docs.title: The Town
docs.text: The BS-X town is a 2D top-down village divided into several districts. The player enters the town from Ransei Bridge (らんせい橋), which spans across a river at the town's entrance. The Satellaview History Museum is one of the few sources that documented the town's map layout.1

docs.title: Ransei Bridge (らんせい橋)
docs.text: The starting point of the game. The bridge crosses a river at the town's entrance and serves as the primary gateway. This is where the player first arrives and begins their exploration.2

docs.title: Town Square (中央広場)
docs.text: The central hub of the town, connecting to all major districts. The town square features: - A central fountain or monument - Benches where NPCs occasionally sit - Access to all directional paths3

docs.title: Download Center (ダウンロードセンター)
docs.text: Located off the town square, this building is where players browse and download broadcasted games and data. An elderly NPC manages the service and provides information about available downloads.4

docs.title: Event Plaza (イベント広場)
docs.text: A dedicated area for time-limited downloadable content. During active broadcasts, special events, competitions, and promotions were hosted here. The content was updated via satellite on a regular schedule.5

docs.title: Memory Pack Station
docs.text: A management interface for the Memory Pack, allowing players to view, delete, and organize saved content. Located in a dedicated building.6

docs.title: Magazine Stand (雑誌スタンド)
docs.text: Where players could access downloaded game magazines, "kabe shinbun" (wall newspaper) content, and news updates delivered via satellite.7

docs.title: Fortune Teller's Stall
docs.text: A small booth where a fortune teller NPC provides information about upcoming broadcast schedules and sometimes cryptic hints about future content.8

docs.title: Residential Areas
docs.text: The town includes residential districts with houses that NPCs inhabit. Some buildings are purely decorative; others serve minor functions or contain NPCs who provide flavor dialogue. The town's layout suggests it was designed to feel lived-in despite its primarily functional purpose as an operating system.9

docs.title: Seasonal Decoration
docs.text: The town would change its appearance based on: - Seasonal events -- decorations for holidays (Christmas, New Year, etc.) - Special broadcasts -- banners or signs announcing major content drops - Time of day -- lighting and NPC behavior changes10

docs.title: The Name-Theft Mystery
docs.text: Throughout the town, signs and banners with the town's name are conspicuously blank or obscured. NPCs comment on this, referencing the central premise: the town's name was stolen. The player's exploration and participation in broadcasts gradually uncover the story behind the theft, though how much of this narrative was planned versus emergent from the service's structure is unclear.11

docs.title: Unknown Locations
docs.text:
Due to the loss of original documentation and the time-limited nature of some events, not all locations in the BS-X town have been documented. Some areas may have been added or modified during the service's lifetime via satellite updates and are now lost.12

docs.title: What is SoundLink?
docs.text: SoundLink was the Satellaview's signature feature: games that synchronized gameplay with live radio broadcasts. Players would tune into St.GIGA's satellite audio channel while playing, and the game would respond to the broadcast in real time.1

docs.title: How SoundLink Worked
docs.text:
The SoundLink system required:

  1. Satellaview hardware connected to the Super Famicom
  2. BS-X cartridge with the Memory Pack inserted
  3. Satellite dish tuned to BS-5 channel
  4. St.GIGA subscription for the data broadcast service
  5. Radio receiver (or TV with satellite tuner) for the audio portion

The game cartridge contained the base gameplay code, but key elements were triggered by the broadcast signal. During designated "SoundLink" periods, the game would:2

  • Receive timing signals from the satellite to synchronize with radio audio
  • Display visual cues corresponding to radio narration
  • Enable special events and content only during broadcast windows
  • Track player performance for broadcast leaderboards

docs.title: Live Narration
docs.text:
Radio personalities would narrate gameplay, provide backstory, and guide players through levels. This was especially prominent in:

  • BS Zelda: Ancient Stone Tablets -- full voice acting for characters
  • BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki -- radio drama segments between battles
  • BS Tantei Club: Yuki ni Kieru Kako -- narrated mystery segments

docs.title: Music Broadcasts
docs.text: St.GIGA broadcast music that was synchronized with gameplay. The music changed week-to-week in multi-episode games. Music restoration projects have attempted to recover these broadcasts from VHS recordings.3

docs.title: Sound Effects
docs.text: Some SoundLink games incorporated broadcast audio as dynamic sound effects -- enemy roars, environmental sounds, or event cues that were not present in the base ROM data.

docs.title: The Ephemeral Nature of SoundLink
docs.text: SoundLink games were inherently time-limited experiences: - They could only be played during designated broadcast windows - Gameplay could not be saved (the game existed in RAM, not the Memory Pack) - Rebroadcasts were rare and sometimes altered4 - Most SoundLink content is lost forever because recordings were not officially preserved

docs.title: Audio Preservation
docs.text:
Fan preservation of SoundLink audio has taken several approaches:

  1. VHS recordings -- Fans recorded broadcasts to VHS tape, capturing both the video output and audio. These tapes have been the primary source for audio restoration5
  2. Audio splicing -- Extracting "clean" portions of songs from VHS recordings and splicing them into contiguous wholes6
  3. Album sources -- Some Satellaview music was released on official soundtrack albums (e.g., BS Zelda music was available on Zelda soundtrack releases)7
  4. Fan recreation -- Using audio tools to recreate Satellaview music based on known compositions, notably via Nico Nico Douga (for BS Fire Emblem music)8

docs.title: The St.GIGA Audio Experience
docs.text: Beyond game audio, St.GIGA broadcast ambient music and personality segments. St.GIGA Forever documented the ambient music portions of St.GIGA's broadcasts, which included a distinctive soundscape that merged Japanese radio aesthetics with experimental electronic music.9

docs.title: Where to Experience SoundLink Today
docs.text: While the original broadcasts are long gone, several recordings survive online:

docs.title: BS Zelda Series
docs.text:
• BS Zelda Map 1 — original broadcast gameplay (YouTube, uploaded by makuchan): shows how a SoundLink download worked with live narration10
  • BS Zelda Map 1 — annotated complete run (YouTube, 4 parts): subtitled gameplay with preserved voice acting11
  • BS Zelda: Ancient Stone Tablets — week 4 voice acting translation (BS Zelda Shrine): full transcript with video of the original broadcast narration12
  • BS Zelda: Ancient Stone Tablets — all weeks (NicoVideo): complete broadcast recordings with voice acting, discovered 200713

docs.title: BS Fire Emblem: Akaneia Senki
docs.text:
All 4 episodes of the original broadcast survive on video:

  • Episode 1 — complete broadcast with radio drama segments and live commentary14
  • Episode 2 — "Red Wind Ron", mirrored on Satellablog15
  • Episodes 3 & 4 — complete finale, uploaded 2010 after the DS remake announcement16

docs.title: Other SoundLink Games
docs.text:

  • Satellaview+ (satellaviewplus.github.io): live simulated St.GIGA broadcasts, currently active with emulation client — listen to recreated broadcasts in real time18

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Satellaview (サテラビュー) was a satellite modem peripheral for the Super Famicom, released by Nintendo in 1995 exclusively in Japan. It connected to the console via the expansion port and received data broadcasts via satellite through a partnership with the radio station St.GIGA.1

The system allowed users to download games, magazines, and additional content over satellite during designated broadcast windows. It also featured SoundLink games, which synchronized gameplay with live radio broadcasts including voice narration and music.2

docs.title: Technical Specifications
docs.text:
Component Details Release Date April 23, 1995 (BS-X cartridge launch)3 Price ~¥14,000 (~$150 USD)4 Broadcast Partner St.GIGA (BS analog channel 5)5 Broadcast Hours 4:00 PM - 7:00 PM daily6 Required Accessories BS-X cartridge, Memory Pack (1 megabit flash RAM), satellite antenna subscription

The Satellaview connected to the Super Famicom via its EXT port (the expansion port on the bottom of the console). It required a satellite dish tuned to the BS-5 channel (NHK's satellite channel) and a subscription to St.GIGA's data broadcasting service.7

docs.title: The BS-X Cartridge
docs.text:
The BS-X: Sore wa Namae o Nusumareta Machi no Monogatari (BS-X: The Story of the Town Whose Name Was Stolen) cartridge served as the operating system and user interface for the Satellaview. It was required to boot the system and provided:

  • A graphical town interface where the player could navigate
  • A download manager for receiving broadcasts
  • A memory pack manager for saving content
  • An event plaza for time-limited downloadable content8

The cartridge contained the entirety of the Satellaview's browser/OS software. Without it, the Satellaview hardware was non-functional.9

docs.title: The Memory Pack
docs.text: The Memory Pack was a 1-megabit (128KB) flash RAM cartridge that plugged into the BS-X cartridge (similar in form factor to a Super Game Boy). It stored downloaded games, save data, and configuration settings. The pack used a battery-backed SRAM + flash memory combination and functioned similarly to later Nintendo Power flash carts.10

docs.title: Downloadable Games
docs.text: Full games or add-on data that could be downloaded and played at any time after broadcast. These were stored on the Memory Pack.11

docs.title: SoundLink Games
docs.text: Real-time interactive games that synchronized with live radio broadcasts. These games featured voice acting, commentary, and music that changed week-to-week. SoundLink games could not be saved -- they existed only during the broadcast window.12

docs.title: Magazines and News
docs.text: Downloadable "kabe shinbun" (wall newspaper) content and game magazines that provided news, tips, and game-related articles.13

docs.title: Service Timeline
docs.text: Date Event April 23, 1995 BS-X cartridge and Satellaview service launch<sup>14</sup> 1995-1996 Initial SoundLink broadcasts 1997 Peak of service; major franchises (Zelda, Fire Emblem, Mario) featured 1999 Service begins winding down June 1999 Last regular Satellaview broadcasts<sup>15</sup> Early 2000 St.GIGA dissolves; Satellaview service officially ends<sup>16</sup> March 31, 2005 End of BS analog broadcasting (St.GIGA/WINJ)<sup>17</sup>

docs.title: Business Model Failure
docs.text: The Satellaview's business model was complex: users paid for the hardware, a monthly subscription to St.GIGA, and then the games themselves were "free" during broadcasts. However, Nintendo struggled to attract advertisers and sponsors for broadcasts. The specialized nature of the content and Japan's economic downturn in the late 1990s contributed to the system's commercial failure.18 Nintendo eventually withdrew from the partnership, leaving St.GIGA to continue solo broadcasts until the service's end.19

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
Despite its commercial failure, the Satellaview has become a subject of intense interest among video game preservationists and historians. Many Satellaview-exclusive games were never released through any other medium and today survive only through ROM dumps, VHS recordings of broadcasts, and fan restoration projects.20

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: St.GIGA (セント・ギガ) was a Japanese satellite radio broadcaster that partnered with Nintendo to provide data broadcasting services for the Satellaview. The company was founded in 1991 and began satellite radio broadcasts in 1993 on the BS-5 channel (NHK's satellite channel).1

docs.title: Partnership with Nintendo
docs.text:
St.GIGA's partnership with Nintendo resulted from Nintendo's interest in satellite-based game distribution. Nintendo invested in St.GIGA, and the collaboration produced the Satellaview system, launched in 1995. Under the partnership, St.GIGA provided:2

  • Satellite broadcast infrastructure -- signal transmission, scheduling, and data encoding
  • Radio programming -- live personalities, music, and narration for SoundLink games
  • Subscription management -- user billing for the data broadcasting service
  • Studio facilities -- for producing live radio segments synchronized with gameplay

docs.title: Broadcast Content
docs.text:
St.GIGA's "Super Famicom Hour" was the daily broadcast window (4:00 PM - 7:00 PM) dedicated to Satellaview content. The programming included three pillars:3

  1. Radio programs featuring celebrities including Tamori (talent/show host), Ayumi Hamasaki (singer), and comedy duo Bakusho Mondai
  2. Downloadable original games and add-on data
  3. Sound Link games -- the signature Satellaview format combining radio broadcasts with interactive gameplay

docs.title: Financial Difficulties
docs.text:
The Satellaview's business model proved unsustainable. Key factors:4

  • Inability to attract sufficient advertisers and sponsors
  • Specialized nature of content limiting audience size
  • Japan's economic downturn in the late 1990s
  • High infrastructure costs for satellite broadcasting

Nintendo eventually withdrew from the partnership, leaving St.GIGA to continue solo broadcasts.

docs.title: Post-Satellaview Era
docs.text:
After the Satellaview service ended (~June 1999), St.GIGA continued operating as a satellite radio broadcaster. However, financial difficulties persisted:5

Date Event 2000 St.GIGA dissolves? (sources differ on exact date of dissolution) ~2003 Business transferred to World Independent Networks Japan (WINJ) March 31, 2005 End of BS analog broadcasting ~2006 WINJ broadcasts cease November 2007 WINJ declared legally "bankrupt" (破綻)

The domain stgiga.jp was maintained by fans as a memorial site (St.GIGA Forever) until the early 2020s, when it was redirected to unrelated content.6

docs.title: Personalities
docs.text: St.GIGA employed several notable radio personalities who appeared during Satellaview broadcasts: - Tamori (also known for hosting "Music Station" and "Waratte Iitomo!") -- hosted Tamori no Picross7 - Ayumi Hamasaki -- early in her career, appeared in Satellaview programming - Bakusho Mondai (comedy duo) -- hosted game-related segments

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
St.GIGA's legacy is intrinsically tied to the Satellaview. The company's pioneering work in satellite data broadcasting for video games was ahead of its time but commercially unsuccessful. The dissolution of St.GIGA contributed significantly to the loss of Satellaview archival materials, as corporate records, broadcast masters, and internal documentation were reportedly not preserved.8

docs.title: BS-X Development Team (Nintendo R&D2)
docs.text: The BS-X cartridge was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 2 Division (R&D2), led by general manager Masayuki Uemura.1 R&D2 was responsible for the Satellaview hardware and the BS-X software.

docs.title: Hidden Developer Credits
docs.text:

I'd certainly have no complaints if it got turned into a live-action show and became a much-discussed work like Twin Peaks."9

docs.title: Priority Matrix
docs.text: This page provides a strategic framework for reaching the original BS-X development team members. Unlike the fan community, these individuals are harder to reach but possess the primary knowledge about the system's creation, design intent, and unreleased content.

docs.title: 1. Noriko Kitamura (北村 典子) -- Nintendo Employee
docs.text:
Detail Information Role BS-X Designer, Satebô/Parabô mascot creator Current Still employed at Nintendo (1995-present)1 Recent Work Nintendo World Championship (2024) - Planner Best Contact Method Via Nintendo corporate channels OR professional networking

Strategy: - Contact Nintendo's PR department with a formal interview request - Reference her work on BS-X, SatellaWalker, and the Satellaview mascots - She was featured in an Iwata Asks interview (Jam with the Band) -- demonstrate knowledge of her career - Kyoto Report found her Facebook profile -- a respectful message there may work - Approach as a professional historian, not a fan

Language: Japanese (primary) / may have some English proficiency Risk: Low -- she's a current Nintendo employee, so corporate policies may restrict what she can discuss Alternative: Contact via Nintendo's PR/Communications department

docs.title: 2. Stephen Meyerink -- Translator/Intermediary
docs.text:
Detail Information Role Japanese-to-English translator who worked on Satellaview-Tsushin interviews Contact sjmtaelus.com (contact form available)2 Status Active freelance translator

Strategy: - He already has context on BS-X history (translated the Akamatsu and Miyamoto interviews) - Could help locate Yusuke Akamatsu or facilitate contact - Could translate additional Japanese source materials - Professional relationship already established with Time Extension

Best for: Locating Akamatsu, translating materials, introductions

docs.title: 3. Jack Yarwood -- Time Extension Journalist
docs.text: Strategy: - Wrote the Satellaview feature for Time Extension (2023-2024) - Already interviewed Miyamoto and Akamatsu material - May have contact information for Akamatsu or leads on other sources - Professional journalist -- could collaborate on further research

docs.title: 4. LuigiBlood (via Twitter/GitHub)
docs.text:
• Already well-documented in the Researchers page
  • Has contact with the Japanese preservation community
  • May know how to reach former St.GIGA employees or Japanese developers

docs.title: 5. Yusuke Akamatsu (赤松 裕介) -- BS-X Writer
docs.text:
Detail Information Role BS-X writer, "Super Famicom Happy Hour" producer Last Known 1995 Satellaview-Tsushin interview; fiction writer in the 1990s Status Unknown -- needs to be located

Search Strategy: - He wrote novels under the name Yusuke Akamatsu -- search Japanese book databases (Amazon Japan, Kinokuniya) - Check if he published under "赤松裕介" (note: the Satellaview broadcast list mentions "Akamatsu Yuusuke Theater") - Stephen Meyerink may have leads from the translation work - Japanese publisher contacts for his books ("Scratch of Sun", "I, LOVE YOU, I, MISS YOU") - Search Japanese social media (Twitter Japan, mixi, Facebook)

If found, key questions: - What was the planned ending for BS-X's story? - Was there a BS-X 2 planned? - What happened to the "2010" serialized story? - How did the collaboration with Nintendo R&D2 work? - Are there any story documents or design bibles that survive?

docs.title: 6. Kazuhiko Taniguchi (谷口 和彦) -- Former R&D2 Manager
docs.text:
Detail Information Role Succeeded Uemura as R&D2 GM in 2004; "Old Man Rider" in BS-X credits Status Unknown -- retired from Nintendo?

Search Strategy: - Check if he stayed at Nintendo after the R&D2/SPD merger - Search Japanese professional networks (LinkedIn Japan, Wantedly) - Look for conference appearances or academic involvement (following Uemura's path) - May appear in Japanese game industry alumni networks

Search strategy for each: 1. Search the name + "Nintendo" + "任天堂" on LinkedIn Japan 2. Search for Japanese game conference presentations 3. Check if they appear in other game credits (MobyGames, Kyoto Report) 4. Some may be on Twitter or Facebook

docs.title: Broadcast Data Format
docs.text:
The satellite broadcast data format was reverse-engineered by LuigiBlood for the SatellaWave project. The format includes:7

  • Message Channel -- Text and notification data
  • Directory/Folder/File trees -- Content organization
  • Town Status -- BS-X town state updates
  • Event Plaza expansions -- Time-limited content
  • Patch channels -- Program updates
  • Time channels -- Synchronization data
  • Contest channels -- Competition data (e.g., Bass Fishing No.1)

docs.title: Unresolved Broadcast Data Mysteries
docs.text:
• Many broadcasts were never recorded
  • The "TestData 10/24" ROM (Yuuko Anai no Houkago no Ousama) has a date mismatch between header and actual broadcast date8
  • Official Jupiter Corp broadcast dates for Tamori no Picross (Aug 6-Sep 2, 1995) are contradicted by VHS evidence from April and June 19959

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This page documents what we do not know about BS-X and the Satellaview. These are the open questions, missing pieces, and leads that need to be pursued. Every entry here represents an opportunity for discovery through interviews, archival research, or community outreach.

docs.title: The Unfinished Story
docs.text: Question Details Priority What was the planned ending? Yusuke Akamatsu stated the story was never given a proper ending and was rebooted mid-service. What was the original planned conclusion?<sup>1</sup> ★★★ What was the "2010" side story? Akamatsu serialized a story called "2010" in Satellaview-Tsushin magazine. What did it contain? Where can copies be found?<sup>1</sup> ★★★ How many chapters/episodes were planned? The town's story evolved over the service's lifetime. Was there a specific episode count planned? ★★ Was there a complete narrative bible? Did Nintendo/St.GIGA create a design document or story bible for the town and its characters? ★★★

docs.title: Characters
docs.text: Question Details Priority Who were all the NPCs? We know a handful of NPCs (fortune teller, postman, old man at download center) but not all. A complete NPC roster with names and dialogue is missing. ★★ What did each NPC say? The full dialogue tree of every NPC in the town has not been fully extracted and documented. ★★ Were there time-limited NPCs? Some characters may have appeared only during specific broadcasts or seasons. Which ones, and when? ★★ What was the "mad professor" storyline? Akamatsu mentioned "TV-headed children enchanted by a mad professor" -- what was this subplot?<sup>1</sup> ★★

docs.title: Locations
docs.text: Question Details Priority What is the complete town map? The Satellaview History Museum had a map page, but it was not fully archived. How many screens/locations exist?<sup>2</sup> ★★ Were there secret areas? Were there hidden or unlockable areas in the town that required specific in-game conditions? ★★ Did the town change over time? The Satellaview could update the town via broadcast. What changed between 1995 and 1999? ★★★

docs.title: Items & Currency
docs.text: Question Details Priority What was the full item list? Players could buy telephone cards, vehicle tickets, fish bait, shoes for dashing. What else existed?<sup>3</sup> ★ How did the economy work? How did players earn in-game currency? What was the pricing of items? ★ Were there rare/event-only items? Were some items only available during specific broadcasts? ★★

docs.title: Broadcast Infrastructure
docs.text: Question Details Priority How was the St.GIGA broadcast center set up? What equipment did St.GIGA use to encode and transmit game data? ★★ Where was the St.GIGA studio located? The physical location of the broadcast center is not well documented. ★ How many staff operated the Satellaview service? The size of the Satellaview operations team at St.GIGA is unknown. ★★ What happened to the broadcast servers? After St.GIGA dissolved, what happened to the physical broadcast equipment and data servers? ★★★

docs.title: BS-X Cartridge
docs.text: Question Details Priority Are there different BS-X ROM revisions? Multiple BS-X cartridge revisions may exist. How many, and what changed? ★★ What unused content exists? TCRF documented unused music and text, but the full extent is unknown.<sup>4</sup> ★★ How did the online leaderboard system work? BS-X supported score submission. What was the technical implementation? ★★ Was there anti-piracy/region locking? The BS-X cartridge had DRM that LuigiBlood patched. How did it work?<sup>5</sup> ★

docs.title: Memory Pack
docs.text: Question Details Priority What is the complete list of Memory Pack commercial releases? Nintendo sold pre-loaded Memory Packs. A complete catalog is missing. ★★ How many Memory Packs survive? No census of surviving Memory Packs exists. ★ What data is still undumped? Many Memory Packs likely contain data that has never been dumped.<sup>6</sup> ★★★

docs.title: SoundLink Games
docs.text: Question Details Priority How many SoundLink broadcasts are completely lost? Most SoundLink games were never recorded. An estimate of losses is needed. ★★★ Were there any "lost" major titles? Are there major franchise games that were broadcast but never documented? ★★★ What was the full schedule of every broadcast? The complete broadcast schedule across 1995-1999 is not fully reconstructed.<sup>2</sup> ★★

docs.title: Magazines & Kabe Shinbun
docs.text: Question Details Priority How many magazine issues were broadcast? The full catalog of Satellaview magazine content is unknown. ★★ What did the "kabe shinbun" (wall newspaper) contain? Only fragments have been recovered from recent dumps.<sup>6</sup> ★★ Are there Satellaview-Tsushin back issues? The Satellaview-Tsushin magazine contained developer interviews and side stories. Where are surviving copies? ★★★

docs.title: Audio Content
docs.text: Question Details Priority How much St.GIGA radio audio survives? VHS recordings captured some audio, but the total surviving archive is unknown. ★★★ Were all SoundLink audio tracks lost? The radio narration and music for most SoundLink games exists only in fan recordings.<sup>7</sup> ★★★ What music was exclusive to broadcasts? Some music for BS Zelda, BS Fire Emblem etc. was never released on albums. How much is missing?<sup>8</sup> ★★

docs.title: The ROMar Mystery
docs.text: Question Details Priority Who was ROMar? The single most important anonymous figure in Satellaview preservation. The source of the first ROM leaks. Never identified.<sup>9</sup> ★★★ How did ROMar obtain the ROMs? Were they a St.GIGA employee, a Nintendo contractor, or a collector with insider access? ★★★ What else did ROMar have? Pachuka only leaked a portion of ROMar's collection. What other unreleased material existed? ★★★ Is ROMar still alive? ROMar's current status is completely unknown. ★★★

docs.title: R&D2 Developers (Unknown Status)
docs.text:
Of the ~35 developers in the BS-X hidden credits, only Noriko Kitamura has a confirmed current status (still at Nintendo). The whereabouts of the remaining ~34 developers are unknown. Many would be in their 50s-60s now.

Priority targets for location: - Kazuhiko Taniguchi -- Succeeded Uemura as R&D2 GM. Most likely to have comprehensive knowledge. - Motomu Rikiishi -- Programmer (BS-X + Jupiter Corp). Dual-company perspective. - Masato Furukawa -- Programmer (BS-X + Jupiter Corp). Dual-company perspective. - Katsuya Nakagawa -- "Excavator" Nakagawa. Listed in BS-X credits.

docs.title: Business & Corporate Unknowns
docs.text: Question Details Priority What was Nintendo's total investment? The financial scale of the Nintendo-St.GIGA partnership is unknown. ★★ How many Satellaview units were sold? Estimates vary. St.GIGA claimed 116,378 subscribers at peak in March 1997.<sup>10</sup> But units sold vs. active subscribers is unclear. ★★ What was the internal reaction at Nintendo to its failure? No internal Nintendo post-mortem has ever been made public. ★★★ Was there a successor planned? The SatellaOFF group discussed "BS-X 2" rumors. Was there actually a successor in development?<sup>11</sup> ★★★ Why did Nintendo never release Satellaview content on other platforms? Most Satellaview games were never re-released. What were the legal/technical barriers? ★★

docs.title: Preservation Gaps
docs.text: Gap Details Priority No complete ROM set Not all Satellaview ROMs have been dumped. Some exist only on undumped Memory Packs. ★★★ No complete broadcast schedule A day-by-day schedule of all Satellaview broadcasts 1995-1999 does not exist in any known source. ★★★ No complete item/location database No one has fully catalogued every item, NPC, and location in BS-X. ★★ No developer interview archive Only one Akamatsu interview and one Miyamoto interview from the era are known. ★★★ No St.GIGA corporate archive When St.GIGA dissolved, corporate records were reportedly not preserved. ★★★ No Nintendo internal documents Nintendo has never released internal documents about the Satellaview. ★★★

docs.title: The St.GIGA Bankruptcy: Missing Details
docs.text: Question Details Priority What exactly happened to St.GIGA? The timeline of St.GIGA's dissolution is unclear in multiple sources. Different dates are given for when the company ceased operations.<sup>12</sup> ★★ What was WINJ's role? World Independent Networks Japan took over St.GIGA's assets. What did they do, and why did they also fail?<sup>12</sup> ★★ Were St.GIGA's broadcast tapes preserved? St.GIGA likely had master tapes of all broadcasts. Were they archived or destroyed? ★★★

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The BS-X Project is a long-running fan initiative by LuigiBlood aimed at researching, documenting, emulating, and making accessible the Nintendo Satellaview / BS-X satellite broadcast system. It began in September 2010 under the name "Broadcast Satellaview" and has since become the most comprehensive technical preservation effort for the platform.1

docs.title: SatellaWave
docs.text:
SatellaWave is a Satellaview Server Manager (C#, MIT License) that creates broadcast data binary files (BSX*.bin) for use in emulators. It supports:2

  • Message Channel data
  • Directory/Folder/File tree structures
  • Town Status (BS-X town state)
  • Event Plaza expansions
  • Patch channels
  • Time channels
  • Bass Fishing No.1 contest channels
  • Full bytecode Script engine for BS-X's event system

The latest release is v0.5.1 (March 6, 2019), with the last code push to GitHub in April 2025.3

docs.title: English Translation Patch
docs.text:
The BS-X English Translation Patch translates the entire BS-X town interface including:4

  • Menu systems and navigation
  • Dialog text from all NPCs
  • Item descriptions and signage
  • Event Plaza content

Final version: v1.3 (2016)

A "No DRM" variant removes copy protection checks. The patch is distributed from project.satellaview.org.5

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Satellaview emulation has progressed significantly from the early 2000s to the present day. The unique challenges of the system -- custom mapper, Memory Pack emulation, satellite signal simulation -- have been addressed by multiple projects.

docs.title: bsnes-plus
docs.text:
bsnes-plus provides the most complete Satellaview emulation available in a software emulator. Features include:1

  • Proper BS-X mapper emulation
  • Memory Pack support (including Type 1 Flash commands for Tsukuru games)
  • Satellite signal emulation based on external binary files
  • Memory Pack save/load functionality

Developed as a collaboration between LuigiBlood and Revenant, building on bsnes-sx2 (LuigiBlood's earlier fork).2

docs.title: SNES9X
docs.text: Satellaview support was added to official SNES9X starting from v1.55 (2017). This was the result of upstreaming LuigiBlood's snes9x-sx2 fork into the main emulator codebase.3

docs.title: sd2snes / FX Pak Pro
docs.text: Real-hardware Satellaview emulation via flashcart, supported by: - RAW broadcast data (bsxpage.bin) loaded from SD card - Memory Pack emulation on FPGA - Collaboration between LuigiBlood and ikari_01 (sd2snes developer)4

docs.title: Emulation Requirements
docs.text:
To play Satellaview games in emulation, the following are needed:

  1. BS-X ROM dump -- The BS-X cartridge ROM (required for BIOS)
  2. Broadcast data files -- BSX*.bin files containing the broadcast content
  3. Memory Pack data -- For save file emulation
  4. Emulator with Satellaview support -- bsnes-plus, SNES9X v1.55+, or FX Pak Pro

docs.title: The BS-X BIOS Challenge
docs.text:
The BS-X cartridge uses a custom memory mapper that was not initially understood by emulator developers. The first BS-X BIOS emulation became available on September 24, 2004.5

The "Hello Satellaview!" homebrew (July 2010) by LuigiBlood was a breakthrough, as it required reverse-engineering the BS-X header format including:

  • Satellaview-specific header data at $FFC0
  • Registers $218E-$2192
  • Memory Pack command interface
  • Broadcast data format6

docs.title: Memory Pack Emulation
docs.text:
The Memory Pack presented unique challenges because it used: - Flash memory for game storage (with specific write/erase command sequences) - Battery-backed SRAM for save data - Type 1 Flash commands used by Tsukuru games that differed from standard commands

These were documented by LuigiBlood and integrated into bsnes-plus and SNES9X.7

docs.title: Satellite Signal Simulation
docs.text:
The most complex aspect of Satellaview emulation is simulating the satellite broadcast signal. Two approaches exist:

  1. Pre-recorded data files -- SatellaWave generates BSX*.bin files containing all broadcast data, which the emulator loads as if receiving a satellite signal8
  2. Live server -- The Satellaview+ project provides a simulated St.GIGA server that emulators and real hardware can connect to9

docs.title: Current Status (2026)
docs.text:
• All known Satellaview ROMs are playable on modern emulators
  • The BS-X Project's translation patch makes the interface accessible to English speakers
  • Satellaview+ provides live broadcast simulation
  • Real-hardware playback via FX Pak Pro is supported
  • New dumps are still being released (as recently as 2024-2026)10

docs.title: Satellaview Modem Unit
docs.text: The Satellaview (model SHVC-027) was a satellite modem that connected to the Super Famicom's expansion port (the EXT port on the bottom of the console). It received data broadcasts from the BS-5 satellite channel.1

docs.title: Physical Specifications
docs.text:
Component Description Form factor Cartridge-shaped unit that plugged into the SFC expansion port Connection Super Famicom EXT port (bottom of console) Satellite input F-type connector for satellite dish coaxial cable Power Powered through the Super Famicom console Additional ports Proprietary connector for BS-X cartridge

The unit contained: - Satellite tuner and demodulator - Error correction hardware - Interface logic for the Super Famicom bus2

docs.title: BS-X Cartridge
docs.text:
The BS-X cartridge (the "Town Whose Name Was Stolen") plugged into the top slot of the Satellaview modem unit. It contained:3

  • ROM -- The BS-X operating system and town interface (4 megabits / 512KB)
  • Memory Pack slot -- A slot on the top of the cartridge for the Memory Pack
  • BS-X mapper -- Custom memory mapping hardware for handling satellite data, Memory Pack access, and broadcast signal processing
  • CIC lockout chip -- Standard Nintendo authentication

The cartridge's custom mapper was one of the most complex used on the Super Famicom and was not fully understood by emulator developers until the late 2000s/early 2010s.4

docs.title: Memory Pack
docs.text: The Memory Pack (model SHVC-028) was a 1-megabit (128KB) flash RAM cartridge that plugged into the BS-X cartridge. It used a form factor similar to the Super Game Boy.5

docs.title: Memory Pack Technical Details
docs.text:
Component Specification Storage 1 megabit (128KB) Memory type Flash memory + battery-backed SRAM Flash usage Game and content storage SRAM usage Save data and configuration Interface Via BS-X cartridge mapper Power Battery for SRAM retention

The dual-memory approach (flash for storage, SRAM for saves) was innovative for 1995 but complex to emulate. The flash memory required specific command sequences for write and erase operations that varied between manufacturers.6

docs.title: Nintendo Power / GK Writer System
docs.text:
The Satellaview's Memory Pack was conceptually related to the Nintendo Power rewriteable cart service (known during development as the "Game Kiosk" system). Official documentation from 1997 describes:7

  • GK Controller -- Management unit
  • GK Writer (Master & Slave) -- Flash cart writing stations
  • GK Terminal -- Windows 95 kiosk with 10.4" LCD, thermal printer, PCMCIA slot
  • F Cassette -- 32Mb flash + 256Kb battery-backed SRAM, with ASIC + CIC

The F Cassette used a 32-megabit flash chip split into 28Mb user + 4Mb menu, with plans for 100 titles at launch.8

docs.title: Accessories and Merchandise
docs.text:
St.GIGA and Nintendo produced limited Satellaview-branded merchandise, documented by Satellaview Heaven:

  • Original whistle -- St.GIGA-branded whistle
  • Wristwatch -- featuring Satellaview/St.GIGA logos
  • Various promotional items9

docs.title: History of Satellaview ROM Dumping
docs.text: The history of Satellaview ROM dumping is closely tied to the story of BS-X Cult and the figure known as ROMar. The first Satellaview ROMs to reach the internet were leaked through Pachuka's BS-X Cult site in the late 1990s.1

docs.title: The First Dumps
docs.text:
The earliest known Satellaview ROMs were: - BS Dragon Quest -- a unique debug build with all 4 episodes combined - BS Zelda no Densetsu -- Map 1 and Map 2 - BS Zelda no Densetsu: Inishie no Sekiban -- Ancient Stone Tablets

These were reportedly "stolen" by Pachuka from a hoarder known as ROMar, whose identity remains unknown. The dumps were significant because they represented the first time any Satellaview content had been preserved outside of the original broadcast system.2

docs.title: Hardware Dumping
docs.text:
Most Satellaview ROMs have been dumped using specialized hardware:

  • EPROM programmers adapted for SNES cartridge reading
  • Flash cart readers capable of interfacing with Memory Pack flash memory
  • Custom dumping tools built by preservationists like Matthew Callis3

docs.title: BS-X SRAM Dumping
docs.text: Dumping the battery-backed SRAM (save data) from BS-X Memory Packs proved especially challenging. In 2011, Matthew Callis successfully dumped 22 BS-X SRAM modules, marking the first successful preservation of Satellaview save data after years of technical obstacles.4

docs.title: The Corruption Problem
docs.text: Some dumped ROMs contained corrupted data. LuigiBlood provided detailed corruption analysis, identifying exact byte-level errors. For example, he pinpointed that Map 1 Week 3 had 0x28CC7: 0x02 instead of 0x00. These corruptions were carefully repaired through comparison with known-good copies or reconstruction from broadcast data.5

docs.title: Chaos Seed Satellaview Demo (2024)
docs.text: In June 2024, Matthew Callis dumped the Chaos Seed Satellaview demo -- the first-ever dump of this demo, which was originally streamed on March 11, 1996.6

docs.title: Star Soldier 2-Minute Version
docs.text: Dumped from a Satellaview cartridge that had partially-overwritten BS Zelda data. The ROM required checksum repair through collaboration between multiple preservationists.7

docs.title: Kirby's Toy Box
docs.text: Four minigame cartridges (Circular Ball, Cannon Ball, Pachinko, Arrange Ball) were preserved through a community fundraising effort led by Matthew Callis and Frank Cifaldi. The cartridges were won at auction for ¥85,500 (~$813) and dumped.8

docs.title: Current Dumping Status
docs.text: As of 2026, the Satellablog (maintained by danyl) continues to release regular dumps of: - Memory Pack contents - Broadcast schedules - "Kabe shinbun" (wall newspaper) content - Newly discovered Satellaview cartridges and data9

docs.title: Physical Rarity
docs.text: Satellaview hardware and Memory Packs are increasingly rare. Many Memory Packs have dead batteries or corrupted flash memory.10

docs.title: Data Decay
docs.text: Flash memory in Memory Packs degrades over time. Some dumps show signs of bit rot and require significant reconstruction.

docs.title: Undumped Content
docs.text:
It is believed that some Satellaview broadcasts were never recorded or dumped. SoundLink games, in particular, are almost entirely lost unless they were recorded to VHS by fans during the original broadcasts.11

docs.title: The Satellaview Guide Era
docs.text: Starting in 1997, St.GIGA shifted toward the Satellaview Guide format -- a service providing news, game tips, and magazine-style articles rather than full game downloads. This shift reflected declining investment in the platform and the difficulty of producing regular SoundLink content.1

docs.title: The Final Broadcasts
docs.text: The last regular Satellaview broadcasts occurred around June 1999. The SatellaOFF group's St.GIGA timeline shows Year 5 (April-May 1999) as consisting only of Satellaview Guide content before broadcasts ended entirely.2
